unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 10 gathers the whole of Grade 7 into one evidence-led capstone. You revise thirty review words drawn from Units 1 to 8, from belligerent, alliteration and melancholy to bias, perseverance and claim. Six grammar workshops bring back reported speech, conditionals, the passive voice, relative clauses, verb patterns and the year's compound and participle adjectives. You then reread five review texts, build an enquiry product for a defined audience, defend it for five minutes and reflect on the reader, writer and speaker you have become.
unit.learningPath: Curate and annotate portfolio evidence. Revise the thirty review words and map their connections. Reread five review texts with comprehension checks. Work through six grammar review workshops. Plan, draft and revise the inquiry product. Rehearse, deliver and defend the five-minute presentation. Reflect toward Grade 8 and complete the final course quiz.
howToUse: This is your capstone: one project that draws on the whole year. There is no video — start by reading the project page.
The five readings are review texts from Units 1, 2, 3, 8 and 9. Reread them and answer the comprehension checks.

Writing and Speaking are one enquiry: annotate your portfolio evidence, write the proposal, draft from evidence, revise from feedback, then rehearse and deliver a five-minute presentation and defend it in questions.
The Final course quiz is on this page, after every section has a tick. It is extra — it does not lock the unit.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A complete and often surprising change in the form, appearance or nature of something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The transformation of the draft between March and June was total.
practiceSentences: The transformation of the draft between March and June was total.
What transformation does the character undergo?
A transformation changes the nature of a thing, not only its surface.
Her transformation as a writer began with cutting adjectives.
In mathematics a transformation moves or resizes a shape.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The quality of being well founded and able to stand up to testing.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The validity of the conclusion rests on one unchecked figure.
practiceSentences: The validity of the conclusion rests on one unchecked figure.
How would you test the validity of this argument?
Validity is about the reasoning; truth is about the world.
An argument can have validity and still reach a false conclusion.
A ticket has validity too, which is the everyday use of the word.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: How much something varies from one measurement to the next.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The variability between the two seasons made the average useless.
practiceSentences: The variability between the two seasons made the average useless.
What variability would you expect in this data?
High variability hides a pattern that a mean pretends is there.
She reported the variability alongside the average, as she should.
Variability is how much it changes; a variable is what changes.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: An indirect reference to another work, person or event.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The title is an allusion to an older poem.
practiceSentences: The title is an allusion to an older poem.
Which allusion opens the second stanza?
An allusion rewards the reader who recognises it and does not punish the one who does not.
The speech was full of allusions to the founding story.
An allusion hints at something; a quotation states it.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Placing two things side by side so the contrast shows.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The juxtaposition of the wedding and the funeral is deliberate.
practiceSentences: The juxtaposition of the wedding and the funeral is deliberate.
What does this juxtaposition make you notice?
Juxtaposition argues without saying anything.
The photograph's juxtaposition of new tower and old well says it all.
Juxtaposition places side by side; comparison discusses the difference.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A statement that seems to contradict itself yet holds a truth.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The more you explain the joke, the less funny it is: that is a paradox.
practiceSentences: The more you explain the joke, the less funny it is: that is a paradox.
Which paradox is the poem built around?
A paradox is not a mistake; it is a truth folded awkwardly.
She ended on a paradox and left the audience arguing.
A paradox seems contradictory; a contradiction simply is.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A speech in which a character alone on stage thinks aloud.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The soliloquy lets the audience hear what nobody else may.
practiceSentences: The soliloquy lets the audience hear what nobody else may.
Where does the soliloquy fall in the play?
A soliloquy is spoken alone; an aside is spoken past the others.
His soliloquy runs to forty lines and changes the whole play.
A soliloquy reveals a mind; a dialogue reveals a relationship.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To do with the meaning of words.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The disagreement was semantic: they meant different things by fair.
practiceSentences: The disagreement was semantic: they meant different things by fair.
What semantic difference separates these two words?
A semantic field groups words that share a subject.
She traced the semantic shift of the word across two centuries.
Semantic is about meaning; syntactic is about arrangement.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The arrangement of words to make a well-formed sentence.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The syntax is correct even where the meaning is not.
practiceSentences: The syntax is correct even where the meaning is not.
What does the poet's unusual syntax achieve?
Syntax decides what a sentence can mean before any word is chosen.
Inverted syntax slows a reader down, which may be the point.
Syntax is the order; semantics is the meaning.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The voice a poem is written in, which is not the poet.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The speaker of the poem is a soldier, not the poet herself.
practiceSentences: The speaker of the poem is a soldier, not the poet herself.
What do we learn about the speaker from the first line?
The speaker is a character the poet invents, sometimes unlike them entirely.
Confusing the speaker with the poet is the commonest mistake in essays.
Speaker also means anybody talking, which is why this use has to be taught.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A short, sharp saying that makes its point wittily.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The essay closes on an epigram nobody forgets.
practiceSentences: The essay closes on an epigram nobody forgets.
Which epigram would you choose for the title page?
An epigram must be short enough to repeat from memory.
She wrote an epigram where a paragraph had been.
An epigram is witty and brief; a proverb is old and anonymous.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A play in which the main character is brought down, often by their own flaw.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: A tragedy turns on a flaw in the hero rather than on bad luck.
practiceSentences: A tragedy turns on a flaw in the hero rather than on bad luck.
What flaw brings this tragedy about?
A tragedy ends badly by design, and the audience sees it coming.
The play is a tragedy because the fall could have been avoided.
Tragedy also means any terrible event, which is the everyday use.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To show that two things change together.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The two sets of readings correlate closely.
practiceSentences: The two sets of readings correlate closely.
Does reading time correlate with the results here?
Two things can correlate without either causing the other.
She correlated the rainfall with the harvest over ten years.
To correlate is to move together; to cause is another claim entirely.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To add a limit to a statement so it is not too broad.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Qualify the claim before somebody else does it for you.
practiceSentences: Qualify the claim before somebody else does it for you.
How would you qualify this conclusion?
To qualify a statement is to make it defensible, not to weaken it.
She qualified every finding with the size of the sample.
Qualify also means to become eligible, as for a competition.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To prove that a statement is wrong.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: One counterexample was enough to refute the rule.
practiceSentences: One counterexample was enough to refute the rule.
What evidence would refute this claim?
To refute is to disprove, not merely to deny.
He refuted the argument and conceded the conclusion.
Refute needs evidence; reject needs only an opinion.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To support a claim with evidence.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Substantiate each assertion or remove it.
practiceSentences: Substantiate each assertion or remove it.
What would substantiate this figure?
To substantiate is to show the working, not to repeat the claim.
The article failed to substantiate its most quoted sentence.
Substantiate provides evidence; assert provides none.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To name things one by one in order.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Enumerate the reasons before you rank them.
practiceSentences: Enumerate the reasons before you rank them.
Can you enumerate the steps in the argument?
To enumerate is to list with a number attached.
She enumerated four objections and answered three.
Enumerate names each one; summarise gathers them together.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To take an argument or text apart to see how it works.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Deconstruct the advertisement before you judge it.
practiceSentences: Deconstruct the advertisement before you judge it.
How would you deconstruct this opening paragraph?
To deconstruct is to expose the assumptions holding a thing up.
She deconstructed the speech line by line.
To deconstruct is to take apart; to destroy is not the same word.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Using a grid of numbered axes to give a position.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Cartesian coordinates give every point a pair of numbers.
practiceSentences: Cartesian coordinates give every point a pair of numbers.
Which Cartesian quadrant is this point in?
The Cartesian plane has an x axis and a y axis crossing at zero.
She plotted the results on Cartesian axes.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A fixed relationship in which one quantity scales with another.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The graph shows proportionality between distance and time.
practiceSentences: The graph shows proportionality between distance and time.
Is there proportionality across the whole range?
Proportionality means doubling one doubles the other.
The recipe relies on proportionality, so it scales to any number.
Proportionality is a constant ratio; correlation need not be.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Describing an expression in which the highest power is two.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: A quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
practiceSentences: A quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
Which term makes this equation quadratic?
A quadratic graph is a curve, never a straight line.
She solved the quadratic by completing the square.
Quadratic means squared; linear means to the first power.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Happening or being solved at the same time.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Simultaneous equations are solved together, not one after the other.
practiceSentences: Simultaneous equations are solved together, not one after the other.
What makes these two equations simultaneous?
Two simultaneous equations share a solution that fits both.
The simultaneous broadcasts reached four countries at once.
Simultaneous means at once; consecutive means one then the next.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A statement in mathematics that has been proved from other truths.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The theorem holds for every right-angled triangle.
practiceSentences: The theorem holds for every right-angled triangle.
Which theorem would you use here?
A theorem is proved once and then relied on for ever.
She quoted the theorem rather than reproving it.
A theorem is proved; a conjecture is only believed.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Imagined for the sake of argument rather than real.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Take a hypothetical class of thirty and work it through.
practiceSentences: Take a hypothetical class of thirty and work it through.
Is that a hypothetical case or one that happened?
A hypothetical example tests an argument without accusing anyone.
She answered the hypothetical question and refused the real one.
Hypothetical is supposed for argument; theoretical rests on a theory.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To do with the words of a language rather than its grammar.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The lexical choice between slim and skinny carries the whole judgement.

What lexical field does this poem draw on?
A lexical change alters which words are used, not how they are arranged.

Lexical is about vocabulary; syntactic is about structure.

readings.title: Review text 1: Keeping the Story Alive (Unit 1)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
When Grade 7 began, Unit 1 asked the question that quietly guided our whole year: where do our stories come from? Before you build your capstone portfolio, read this review of that first unit and notice how much of its language you now use with confidence.
In Somali culture, many people can recite their family line back through twenty generations or more. That spoken record, called abtirsiinyo, tells a person their ancestry, their clan, and their place in the community. Across East Africa, other families keep their history alive through songs, spoken stories, and treasured objects handed carefully from one generation to the next.
Historians use precise words for these ways of remembering, and every one of them belongs in your capstone vocabulary. Oral history means knowledge passed down by speaking, often from a grandparent to a listening grandchild. An artefact is an object made by people in the past, such as a carved stool, a woven basket, or a faded photograph. A chronicle is a written record of events arranged in the order they happened. A legacy is what a person leaves behind: values, achievements, skills, or sometimes property. When families experience migration, moving in search of safety or a better life, they often lose houses, land, and possessions. What usually survives the journey is the story itself. A family that knows its heritage carries its identity anywhere, because heritage lives in memory and language as much as in objects.
You may remember Amara, the student whose family interview we studied in September. Her great-grandfather grew coffee and maize on a farm in southern Ethiopia and raised twelve children there. When drought struck in the 1960s, her grandfather walked for three weeks to reach the city with his wife and four children. He worked as a porter at the market while her grandmother sold spices from a small table beside him. Slowly they saved enough money to open a shop, and Amara's father grew up inside it. Amara told the interviewer that the real legacy was never the shop. It was the lesson that hard work and family always come first, even when everything else has been lost.
Notice, as a reviser, how the storytellers of Unit 1 depended on the past simple tense. Verbs such as came, owned, married, walked, and opened carried every completed event in Amara's history. Your capstone biography section will need the same control, along with the present perfect for changes that still matter today.
Here is your review task. Choose one story your own family tells again and again, and list the artefacts, places, and people it protects. Then decide what that story proves about your heritage, and keep the answer ready for the portfolio conference Teacher Yasmin holds this week. One day a younger descendant may ask you where your family began. When that happens, you will understand why Unit 1 called its reading Keeping the Story Alive, and you will have an answer worth passing on.

readings.title: Review text 2: The Hero of Kitale (Unit 2)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Our second unit gave us the story many of you chose as your favourite of the year. Read this condensed retelling, then ask yourself what it taught us about authentic leadership.
Imani rose before the sun on an April morning in Kitale, while her younger brother Kofi still slept on his mat. Their mud-brick house stood near maize farms that spread like a green sea across the land. At school, every teacher said the same thing about her: Imani was diligent, punctual, and utterly dependable. But Imani cared little for praise. She cared about her community, whose water taps were broken and whose library roof had collapsed in the last rainy season.
When her teacher, Mr. Tariq, announced the school's first Student Leadership Election, colourful posters appeared across the compound within days. The loudest candidate was Max, whose uncle owned the largest hardware shop in town. Max handed out sweets, played music through a borrowed speaker at lunchtime, and displayed printed posters instead of handwritten ones. Kofi whispered that Max was legendary. Imani only smiled. She said the school needed a leader who was authentic, not simply loud.
Imani had no money for speakers or printing. She had a notebook, a group of loyal friends, and ideas. Her meticulous hand-drawn posters showed a tree growing from dry ground beside the words: real leaders endure. Her speeches promised no music, only work: a repaired roof and more books. On election day the hall filled with a clamour of voices, and when the votes were counted, Imani had won.
What she did next mattered more than the victory. She stayed late on Thursdays to help younger students with reading, organised a book drive, and helped classmates reconcile after quarrels. When a teacher's motorcycle was stolen, suspicion fell on Kian, a quiet new student. Imani stood in front of the class and insisted he was innocent until proven guilty. The motorcycle was found abandoned near the river the next day, and Kian was cleared. People began to call her a true role model.
A newspaper article followed, then a visit from the county governor, who admired the vegetable garden she had started behind the kitchen. When he asked what inspired her, Imani answered with three values she had lived all year: kindness, honesty, and hard work. Soon afterwards she was invited to speak at the county youth forum, where she told the crowd that waiting for a hero is a mistake. What if you are the one, she asked, and you can change just one thing?
At the end of term, Mr. Tariq handed her a scholarship application for a leadership camp in Nairobi. As her bus left Kitale, Imani watched the maize farms and the newly repaired school roof slide past the window. She did not want fame. She wanted change, and she knew that change takes resilience, diligence, and the courage to lead quietly.
As you plan your capstone speech, borrow Imani's method: fewer promises, more evidence, and a voice the audience can trust.

readings.title: Review text 3: A Voice in the Valley (Unit 3)
readings.theme: Literary expression and the power of voice
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Unit 3 taught us similes, metaphors, and the courage it takes to be read. This retelling of A Voice in the Valley belongs beside your own capstone writing.
In the village of Selota, where mornings began with roosters and the smell of injera, lived a quiet girl named Sana. Her voice was soft, but her imagination was loud. Under her bed she kept a red notebook filled with poems and stories in which trees could walk, rivers could whisper, and the sun signified hope. Her writing overflowed with personification, similes, and metaphors that made the mountains look like sleeping giants. Yet nobody ever read a single page.
Her older brother Zane kept urging her to share it. A voice kept silent, he told her, is like a drum never played. Sana always refused, certain the other students would laugh.
Then her teacher, Miss Alina, announced a school journal and invited every student to submit a story, poem, or article. That night Sana tore two trembling pages from her notebook: a story about a boy who could hear the stars speak. Zane read it and insisted she submit it, so the next morning she dropped it into the submission box before her courage failed.
Weeks passed in silence. Then a poster appeared: the journal, titled Echoes of the Highlands, had been printed, and under a story called Star Listener stood Sana's own name. Students crowded round to read it. A girl named Ivy from another class asked how she had learnt to write with such power. Sana answered honestly: I just listened, and I wrote.
Success changed her quietly. Miss Alina asked her to lead a creative writing session, where Sana used coloured chalk to teach repetition, rhythm, rhyme, and the connotation of words. She showed younger writers how a metaphor such as calling the moon a mirror makes writing richer. She also showed how readers infer meaning from small clues arranged in chronological order. Later she read a new poem at a youth arts event, and a judge declared it should be shared with schools across the region. The next month it was printed in three school newsletters.
The bravest result was not hers. Classmates who had hidden their own work began to submit poems, comics, and essays, and the once-empty writing club grew past twenty members. At the end-of-term ceremony, Sana accepted her certificate beneath a banner reading The Pen Paints What the Voice Feels. She said the award belonged to every quiet voice that dares to speak.
Before your capstone reading this week, return to your own September writing and measure the distance your voice has travelled. Sana's story argues that publishing is not about applause. It is about giving one hidden reader the courage to answer. Decide which of your pieces could do that, and bring it, annotated, to the portfolio conference.

readings.title: Review text 4: The Duty of Truth (Unit 8)
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Unit 8 asked how rules are made and how facts defeat rumours. This retelling of The Duty of Truth will sharpen the source-checking habits your capstone defence depends on.
The trouble at Bahari Secondary School began with a notice that appeared abruptly on the board after the mid-term break. All Form 3 students, it announced, must now report for Saturday cleaning duty, and attendance is mandatory. Zara read it with folded arms. As the liaison between the student council and the school board, she knew a decision made without explanation would breed resentment. Her class had actually contributed the most during the last clean-up day, whatever the rumours claimed.
The council met under the neem tree at lunch. Their secretary, Dina, proposed a formal letter requesting an amendment to the rule, and the group agreed to gather signatures. Zara went further and visited the deputy head teacher to ask for the reasoning. He explained that parents had complained and that the board considered the duty a necessary policy. When she pointed out that students had never been informed, he leaned back and said the matter was not up for debate.
So the students answered with evidence instead of anger. Their letter suggested rotating the duty fairly across all forms and included the participation logs proving Form 3 had not been negligent. By Friday more than two hundred students had signed the petition. That weekend they held a quiet assembly in the school field with signs reading Shared Duty is Fair Duty. By Monday a new notice announced that the rule was paused for review.
The board then invited a student representative to its monthly meeting, and Zara was chosen. In the formal conference room, a senior member asked why students opposed cleaning. She replied that they opposed unfair allocation, not cleaning itself. When another member repeated an anonymous claim that Form 3 had skipped duty before, she answered that a claim is not evidence, and the records agreed with her. The principal confirmed that Form 3 had cleaned more consecutively than any other form, and the room fell silent. A rotating schedule was drafted, partly by Zara herself.
The habit spread. When a student was accused of vandalising a locker simply because he had been nearby, Zara insisted that nobody should be punished on what is merely alleged. A hearing reviewed the testimonies, discovered that a loose screw had caused the damage, and exonerated him completely.
By the end of term the council ran its own newsletter and corresponded regularly with the board. Zara's conclusion belongs in every capstone: progress is not made by big speeches alone. It is made by organising voices, checking facts, and believing that fair structure can serve justice, even when the story starts with a mop and a notice board.

readings.title: Review text 5: Smart Farms and Digital Dreams (Unit 9)
readings.theme: The Digital World and Future Innovation
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Your final review text returns to Unit 9, where young innovators proved that problem-solving is a language skill too. Read it once for meaning, then again for the reported speech and conditional sentences it quietly contains.
In recent years, digital technology has begun to reveal new possibilities for communities across East Africa. From crowded capital cities to small farming towns, young people are finding versatile ways to use smartphones, sensors, and coding to solve problems that once seemed impossible. One of the most exciting areas of change is future farming, which means using technology to grow more food with fewer resources.
In one farming town, a group of secondary-school students noticed that unpredictable rainfall was ruining harvests and pushing food prices higher every season. They decided to acquire basic coding skills and build a simple weather-monitoring app. Their teacher, Mr. Rohan, introduced them to rudimentary electronics: small sensors that measure temperature, humidity, and soil moisture.
Not everyone believed in them. A local shopkeeper said that students were too young to build anything useful and that technology would never replace hard work. The team refused to be discouraged by the criticism. They determined that if they worked together, they could prove the doubters wrong. Unless they tried, they would never know what was possible.
Within three months they had a working prototype. Sensors in the soil sent readings to the app, and the app sent alerts to farmers' phones. If the soil became too dry, the farmer received a warning to water the crops. One farmer reported that an early alert from the app had just saved her entire field of maize. Word spread quickly, and people from neighbouring villages converged on the school to watch demonstrations.
A journalist from a regional radio station asked the team how they had learnt to code. The team leader replied that they had taught themselves using free online tutorials. She added that anyone with a phone and internet access could learn the same skills. The project soon introduced a drone that photographed fields from above, so the students could compare images over time and spot which crops were struggling. That kind of analysis, once obscure and expensive, had become possible for a school team with basic equipment.
Mr. Rohan told a visiting teacher that if the government supported similar programmes, thousands of farms could benefit. He warned that unless young people were given opportunities to innovate, the country would fall behind. Today the app serves more than two hundred farmers across three districts, and the team is building a solar-powered irrigation system next.
As the team leader liked to say, technology is not magic; it is people solving problems, step by step. Your capstone enquiry asks for exactly that spirit: a clear question, honest evidence, and the perseverance to finish.

grammar.title: Reported speech across the year (Units 8 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Reported speech moves a speaker's words into the past: pronouns shift, and the present perfect becomes the past perfect.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Direct: Nora said, "I have just finished my draft." Reported: Nora said that she had just finished her draft. Use say without an object and tell with one: she told me that the article was ready. Time words shift too: today becomes that day, and tomorrow becomes the next day.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers keep the original pronoun and tense, producing Nora said that I have finished, which reports nobody accurately.
grammar.memoryTip: Step back one tense, swap the pronouns, and imagine retelling yesterday's conversation to someone who missed it.
grammar.practice: Part A: Report these lines from the portfolio conferences. Amal said, "I have just chosen my strongest essay." Nora said, "We are rehearsing the defence today." Sami said, "My sources will surprise you." Part B: Find two examples of reported speech in Review text 5 and rewrite each one as a direct quotation. Part C: Report one piece of spoken feedback a partner gave you this week, using told, the way Amal reported Adam's advice: Adam told her that her opening needed a question. Answer key: Part A — Amal said that she had just chosen her strongest essay. Nora said that they were rehearsing the defence that day. Sami said that his sources would surprise me (the pronoun "you" shifts to match whoever heard him say it — swap in the right name or pronoun for your own listener). Part B is answerable straight from Review text 5, which prints its reported speech in full — two examples: "A local shopkeeper said that students were too young to build anything useful and that technology would never replace hard work" becomes The shopkeeper said, "You are too young to build anything useful, and technology will never replace hard work." "The team leader replied that they had taught themselves using free online tutorials" becomes The team leader replied, "We taught ourselves using free online tutorials." (Other valid pairs exist in the same text, such as the farmer's and Mr. Rohan's lines.) Part C reports your own partner's spoken feedback, so there is no fixed line to match — as a self-check, confirm you used told with an object (told me/him/her), stepped the tense back one place, and swapped every pronoun to fit the new speaker, the way the example already models: Adam told her that her opening needed a question.

grammar.title: Conditionals with if and unless (Units 8 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: The first conditional pairs a present-tense condition with a future result, and unless means if not.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: If you check your sources, your argument will stand firm. Unless you water the seedlings, they will die. The comma appears when the condition comes first: If the soil dries out, the app sends an alert. The app sends an alert if the soil dries out.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers put will in both halves, producing If you will check, which doubles the future and breaks the pattern.
grammar.memoryTip: Unless carries its own not, so never add another negative to the same clause.
grammar.practice: Part A: Complete these capstone warnings. If I rehearse twice, ... Unless my evidence is attributed, ... If the audience asks a hard question, ... Part B: Find the two unless sentences in Review text 5 and explain what each one predicts. Part C: Write one first-conditional promise about your Grade 8 reading habits. Answer key: Part A has many correct completions since you choose the ending, but each must keep the pattern If/Unless + present simple, + will + base verb — for example: If I rehearse twice, I will feel more confident. Unless my evidence is attributed, my argument will lose credibility. If the audience asks a hard question, I will pause before I answer. Part B: Review text 5 contains exactly two unless sentences. "Unless they tried, they would never know what was possible" predicts that the students would never discover what their app could do if they gave up before testing it. "Unless young people were given opportunities to innovate, the country would fall behind" predicts that a country that fails to support young innovators risks losing ground to others. (Both sit inside past-tense narration, so would replaces will — the same backshift as reported speech.) Part C is your own promise about Grade 8, so there is no fixed line to check — as a self-check, confirm your sentence keeps the if-clause in the present simple and puts exactly one will in the result clause, matching If I read for twenty minutes every night, I will finish at least two novels each term.

grammar.title: The passive voice: present, past and modal (Units 3, 4, 5 and 7)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: The passive turns attention from the doer to the action: the form of be changes tense while the past participle stays.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Present: cotton is grown before it is spun and woven. Past: the school roof was repaired during the holidays. Modal: every source must be checked, and quotations should be attributed. Add by only when the doer truly matters: the poem was chosen by the judges.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers drop the form of be, producing the roof repaired last term, which reads as an unfinished sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: Find be plus a past participle; if you can add by someone after the verb, the sentence is passive.
grammar.practice: Part A: Turn these active sentences into the passive. Farmers plant maize in March. The council paused the rule. Students must check every claim. Part B: Underline three passives in your own capstone draft, or add them where the doer is unknown. Part C: Explain why Review text 4 says the rule was paused rather than naming who paused it. Answer key: Part A — Maize is planted in March (by farmers). The rule was paused (by the council). Every claim must be checked (by students). Part B is your own capstone draft, so there is no fixed list to check — as a self-check, confirm each passive you underlined or added pairs a form of be with a past participle, and that you only added by someone where the doer truly matters. Part C is answerable from Review text 4: the notice says the rule was paused rather than naming who paused it because the announcement speaks for the school administration as a whole rather than one named decision-maker — the focus stays on the result students cared about (the rule stopping) rather than on which individual signed off on it.

grammar.title: Relative clauses, defining and non-defining (Units 1, 2 and 3)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies its noun, while a non-defining clause adds extra detail between commas.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Defining: the story that won the vote opens our anthology. Non-defining: Sana, who rarely spoke first, taught the writing session. Use who for people, which for things, and whose for possession: the girl whose poem was printed. Never use that after a comma.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers wrap a defining clause in commas, turning the poster that Imani drew into a puzzling aside.
grammar.memoryTip: Cover the clause with your finger; if the sentence loses its meaning, the clause defines and needs no commas.
grammar.practice: Part A: Combine each pair into one sentence. Imani drew posters. The posters showed a growing tree. Zara wrote a report. Zara led the council. Part B: Add one non-defining clause about Mr. Rohan to a sentence from Review text 5. Part C: Write two sentences about your portfolio, one with a defining clause and one with a non-defining clause. Answer key: Part A — Imani drew posters that showed a growing tree (defining — the clause identifies which posters, so no commas). Zara, who led the council, wrote a report (non-defining — Zara is already named, so the clause only adds extra detail and sits inside commas). Part B asks you to add your own clause to a Review text 5 sentence, so there is no single fixed answer — model example: Mr. Rohan, who introduced the team to their first electronics skills, later warned a visiting teacher that the country would fall behind without support for young innovators. Part C is about your own portfolio, so there is no fixed list to check — as a self-check, confirm your defining clause has no commas and could not be removed without losing meaning, and your non-defining clause sits inside commas and could be deleted without confusing the reader.

grammar.title: Verb patterns: gerunds, infinitives and multi-word verbs (Units 3, 5, 7 and 9)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Some verbs take the -ing form, others take to plus the infinitive, and multi-word verbs carry meanings their parts cannot.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Enjoy, finish and practise take -ing: she enjoys revising aloud. Decide, hope and plan take to: they decided to build an app. Multi-word verbs shift meaning: throw away old drafts, carry on revising, and look up every doubtful word.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers mix the patterns, producing she decided applying or he enjoys to argue, which no pattern allows.
grammar.memoryTip: Learn the verb and its partner together, the way Unit 7 paired decide with to and enjoy with -ing.
grammar.practice: Part A: Choose the correct form. She finished (to write / writing) her reflection. We plan (to present / presenting) on Thursday. He kept (to check / checking) his sources. Part B: Replace the plain verbs in these lines with multi-word verbs: discard the weak evidence; continue rehearsing; examine the word in a dictionary. Part C: Write three sentences about your capstone week using one gerund, one infinitive and one multi-word verb. Answer key: Part A — She finished writing her reflection. We plan to present on Thursday. He kept checking his sources. Part B — discard the weak evidence becomes throw away the weak evidence; continue rehearsing becomes carry on rehearsing; examine the word in a dictionary becomes look up the word. Part C is your own capstone-week sentences, so there is no fixed list to check — as a self-check, confirm one sentence uses a gerund after a verb like enjoy, finish or practise, one uses a to-infinitive after a verb like decide, hope or plan, and one uses a multi-word verb such as throw away, carry on or look up, each kept with its correct partner rather than mixed the way the common-mistake note warns against.

grammar.title: Compound and participle adjectives: the final polish (Unit 2)
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Compound adjectives join words with hyphens before a noun, and participle adjectives choose between -ed feelings and -ing causes.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Compound: a five-minute defence, a well-organised portfolio, hand-drawn posters. Participle: the audience felt inspired because the speech was inspiring; a bored listener signals a boring opening. During your final edit, check hyphens, agreement, punctuation and paragraphing in one slow, careful pass.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers pin the -ed form on the cause, calling a slow film bored when the film itself is boring.
grammar.memoryTip: The -ed form belongs to the person who feels; the -ing form belongs to whatever causes the feeling.
grammar.practice: Part A: Hyphenate where needed: a five minute talk, a two hundred signature petition, a solar powered pump. Part B: Choose the correct participle. The results were (surprised / surprising). We felt (encouraged / encouraging) by the feedback. Part C: Complete the final editing checklist on your capstone draft, then read every corrected sentence aloud before you submit. Answer key: Part A — a five-minute talk; a two-hundred-signature petition; a solar-powered pump. Part B — The results were surprising (the results cause the surprise). We felt encouraged (we experience the feeling). Part C is your own final edit of your capstone draft, so there is no fixed list to check — as a self-check, confirm you gave each item on the checklist (hyphens, agreement, punctuation, and paragraphing) its own separate pass, and that you read every corrected sentence aloud, following the memory tip's advice to catch what the eye alone misses.

speaking.title: Portfolio evidence conference

speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me why I chose each of my four portfolio pieces and push me to quote precise evidence from them.

speaking.title: Comparative reading and interpretation

speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Count the review words I use correctly during my explanation and stop me whenever one sounds forced.

writing.title: Portfolio evidence annotations
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write one precise paragraph about each of four selected pieces, explaining what the piece proves about your growth this year.
writing.modelText: This revised report shows that I can organise evidence, evaluate a viewpoint and explain the effect of my choices.
writing.expectedLength: Four short annotation paragraphs, one per piece

items: Piece 1 — My Family Biography (Unit 1, Writing 1): This piece proves I can organise a five-paragraph biography and control past simple narrative tense. The line "Aran's mother, whose name was Dina, kept the household together" shows I could build a defining relative clause without losing the sentence's flow, something I could not do reliably in September.

Piece 2 — Eco-Project Report (Unit 3, Writing 1): This piece proves I can support a persuasive claim with real numbers instead of vague opinion. The sentence "Fifty-eight of the sixty-three garments collected were successfully repaired" shows I had learned to replace words like "lots" with evidence a reader can actually check.

Piece 3 — Fake News Analysis (Unit 8, Writing 2): This piece proves I can evaluate a source's reliability rather than just its content. Naming the missing evidence — "no document, statement or data" — shows I could identify exactly why an unnamed source cannot be trusted.

Piece 4 — Debate Essay: Helping or Harming? (Unit 9, Writing 1): This piece proves I can build an argument using conditional sentences and acknowledge an opposing view fairly. The sentence "Some parents have said that coding is a waste of time... that view is understandable, but adequate limits solve most of the problems" shows I could represent a different opinion honestly before answering it.

writing.successCriteria: Each annotation names the unit, quotes one detail and states clearly what the evidence proves.
writing.support: Use the annotation frame: name the piece, quote it, explain the growth it shows.
writing.extension: Rank your four pieces and justify which one belongs at the front of the portfolio.

writing.title: Inquiry proposal
writing.promptAndInstructions: Propose your enquiry: state the question, the audience, the approved sources and the product you plan to build.
writing.modelText: My enquiry asks how young people in our region can spot misleading headlines before sharing them.
writing.expectedLength: Four organised paragraphs covering question, audience, sources and plan

items: Question: My enquiry question is: How can students at my own school learn to recognise a misleading headline before they share it? I chose this question because our Unit 8 reading about fake news showed me that many people share stories out of alarm rather than evidence, and I want to know whether a short checklist changes that habit.

Audience: My audience is the sixty or so Year 7 and Year 8 students who use our school's group chats every day, since they are the people most likely to share an unverified story within minutes of seeing it.

Sources: My approved sources are: the Ministry of Education's media-literacy guidance (published March 2026), two verified news articles about a real local rumour, and a short survey I will run with twenty classmates during registration week.
Plan: My planned product is a one-page checklist poster, written in plain language, that I will pin up near the library noticeboard and share as a digital image in the main school group chat.

writing.successCriteria: The question is answerable, the audience is defined, and every planned source is named and dated.
writing.support: Choose from the enquiry organiser's question stems and the approved source list.
writing.extension: Add a risk paragraph predicting what could go wrong and how you will adapt.

writing.title: Evidence-led first draft
writing.promptAndInstructions: Draft the full capstone product with cohesive sections, attributed evidence from your source record and a working conclusion.
writing.modelText: Taken together, the sensor data and the farmer interviews suggest that early warnings change real decisions.
writing.expectedLength: Five to seven cohesive paragraphs with attributed source evidence

items: Introduction: Taken together, the Ministry's media-literacy guidance and my own classmate survey suggest that most students do not lack the ability to check a story — they simply never think to try.

Evidence 1: According to the Ministry of Education's guidance (March 2026), a claim is far more likely to be shared unchecked when it uses urgent language such as "BREAKING" or names no clear source. My survey of twenty classmates found that fourteen of them said they had shared at least one story in the past month without checking where it came from.

Evidence 2: The two verified news articles I studied both showed the same pattern: a rumour spread fastest in the first hour, before any official source had time to respond, which matches what happened locally when a false claim about a school closure circulated last term.

Evidence 3, attribution: When I asked classmates why they shared stories quickly, twelve said they simply had not thought to check, rather than that they trusted the source specifically. This suggests the problem is a missing habit, not a lack of care.

Working conclusion: Taken together, this evidence suggests that a short, memorable checklist, placed where students already look — the group chat and the library noticeboard — could close that habit gap more effectively than a single lesson ever could.

writing.successCriteria: Every claim is followed by evidence, every source is attributed, and sections connect with clear transitions.
writing.support: Build each section from the planning frame: claim, evidence, attribution, explanation.
writing.extension: Draft an alternative opening and test both openings on a partner before choosing.

writing.title: Substantive revision from feedback
writing.promptAndInstructions: Record four feedback points from your conferences, then rewrite the sections they target and label each change.
writing.modelText: Feedback said my second claim lacked support, so I added the participation-log detail and named its source.
writing.sentenceStarter: One substantial improvement I made was...
writing.expectedLength: The revised paragraphs plus one summary paragraph of changes

items: Feedback point 1: My partner said my survey number felt vague. Change: I replaced "most students admitted to sharing quickly" with "fourteen of twenty classmates surveyed admitted sharing at least one unchecked story in the past month."

Feedback point 2: My teacher said my introduction did not state a clear question. Change: I added the sentence "My enquiry question is: how can students at my own school learn to recognise a misleading headline before they share it?" as the opening line.

Feedback point 3: A reader said my conclusion repeated the introduction instead of adding anything new. Change: I rewrote the conclusion to recommend a specific product — a one-page checklist poster — instead of simply restating the problem.

Feedback point 4: My teacher said I had not named where the Ministry guidance came from. Change: I added "(Ministry of Education, published March 2026)" the first time I referred to it, and repeated the date wherever I quoted it again.

Summary paragraph: Together, these four changes strengthen the product because each one replaces something vague — a number, a question, a conclusion, a source — with something a reader can actually check, which is exactly the habit my whole enquiry is trying to teach other students to build.

writing.successCriteria: All four feedback points produce visible changes, and the summary explains why each revision strengthens the product.
writing.support: Use the revision log: feedback heard, change made, effect achieved.
writing.extension: Reject one piece of feedback politely in writing and defend your original choice with evidence.

writing.title: Presentation and defence notes
writing.promptAndInstructions: Prepare concise cue cards for the five-minute presentation and the question defence that follows it.
writing.modelText: Card one: hook question. Card two: claim with source. Card three: counterargument. Card four: closing line.
writing.expectedLength: Eight cue cards, each holding one short paragraph or less

items: Card 1 (hook question): "How many of you have shared a story you never actually checked?"
Card 2 (claim with source): 14/20 classmates surveyed shared an unchecked story this month (my survey, June 2026).
Card 3 (claim with source): Ministry guidance: urgent language + no named source = warning sign (Ministry of Education, March 2026).
Card 4 (evidence): Local rumour about school closure spread within one hour, before any official reply.
Card 5 (counterargument): Some say a checklist won't change habits — but 12/20 said they simply hadn't thought to check, not that they didn't care.
Card 6 (product): One-page checklist poster — library noticeboard + group chat image.
Card 7 (limitation): Small sample size — twenty classmates, one school, one term.
Card 8 (closing line): "Checking a story takes one minute. Believing a false one can cost a lot more."

writing.successCriteria: Cards carry key phrases rather than full sentences, and every quoted figure names its source.
writing.support: Number the cards to match the presentation order and mark where to pause.
writing.extension: Prepare two spare cards answering the hardest questions you hope nobody asks.

writing.title: Grade 7 reflection
writing.promptAndInstructions: Evaluate your year honestly: your strongest progress, one stubborn challenge and one specific Grade 8 goal.
writing.modelText: I became a stronger critical reader this year because I learnt to test every claim against its evidence.
writing.expectedLength: Three reflective paragraphs covering progress, challenge and goal

items: Progress: This year I learned to become a stronger critical reader, because I trained myself to test every claim against its evidence instead of trusting confident-sounding language. My Fake News Analysis in Unit 8 is proof of that: in September I would probably have believed the fake claim about schools switching to online-only learning, but by the end of the year I could name exactly which missing details made it untrustworthy.

Challenge: The challenge I still find hardest is organising a long piece of writing into clearly connected sections rather than a list of separate ideas. My capstone first draft needed real feedback before its paragraphs actually built on each other instead of simply sitting side by side.

Goal: My specific goal for Grade 8 is to plan every long piece of writing with a one-line summary of each paragraph before I start drafting, so that connections between sections are decided in advance rather than fixed afterwards during revision.

writing.successCriteria: Each paragraph quotes real evidence from the portfolio, and the Grade 8 goal is specific and measurable.
writing.support: Reread your September work first, then your capstone, and describe the distance between them.
writing.extension: Write a short letter of advice to a student starting Grade 7 in September.

activities.title: Curate and annotate evidence
activities.instructionsAndItems: Reread your work from Units 1-9 and choose four pieces: one reading response, one story or essay, one grammar edit and one recorded talk. For each piece, note the unit it came from and one sentence of evidence that shows growth.
activities.answerSummary: Four pieces are chosen across different units, and each note quotes evidence rather than merely praising it.

activities.title: Build a research word map
activities.instructionsAndItems: Sort the thirty review words into groups you design, such as feelings, argument tools and sound devices. Name each group, then write one sentence explaining a connection between two words from different groups.
activities.answerSummary: Any defensible grouping earns credit; the bridge sentence must use both words accurately.

activities.title: Investigate and verify sources
activities.instructionsAndItems: Choose three passages from the five review texts and record for each: the title, the type of text, one fact it states and one opinion it contains. Then decide which passage earns the most trust and note two reasons.
activities.answerSummary: Facts and opinions are correctly separated, and the trust judgement cites text features rather than preference.

activities.title: Peer review studio
activities.instructionsAndItems: Exchange drafts with a partner. Using the writing rubric, give four specific suggestions about evidence, cohesion, vocabulary and audience effect, and collect four suggestions about your own draft.
activities.answerSummary: Suggestions must name a sentence or section; vague praise does not count.

activities.title: Rehearse with timing
activities.instructionsAndItems: Rehearse your five-minute presentation twice. After the first run, mark where you rushed or stalled; after the second, note one improvement in pace, one in emphasis and one in transitions.
activities.answerSummary: Two timed rehearsals are logged with three named improvements between them.

activities.title: Exhibition and defence
activities.instructionsAndItems: Present your enquiry product at the class exhibition, answer audience questions, then write one Grade 8 learning goal on your reflection card before leaving.
activities.answerSummary: Delivery, defence and a specific written Grade 8 goal complete the milestone.

assignments.title: Grade 7 enquiry capstone and oral defence
assignments.instructions:
Submit the evidence-led enquiry product, attributed source record, four annotated portfolio pieces, five-minute oral defence recording and Grade 8 transition reflection.
Marking guidance for the teacher. Award the 72 marks as follows. Inquiry product, 16 marks: the four writing rubric criteria, four marks each. Oral defence, 16 marks: the four speaking rubric criteria, four marks each, judged on answering for the work rather than presenting it. Attributed source record, 16 marks: 4 for completeness, 4 for accurate attribution, 4 for evaluating reliability, 4 for showing where each source changed the conclusion. Four annotated portfolio pieces, 16 marks: 4 each, awarded for naming the unit, naming the skill and giving a real reason. Reflection, 8 marks: 4 for an honest account of what changed, 4 for a specific and reachable transition goal. Do not award marks for presentation polish or for the materials a family can afford. Assess the English and the reasoning only, and accept scribed or recorded work where a learner needs it.

quizzes.question: Which review word from Unit 1 means 'to make someone very angry'?
quizzes.explanation: To infuriate someone is to make them very angry; acknowledge, endeavour and demonstrate carry no sense of anger.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses a participle adjective correctly?
quizzes.options: The film was bored, so we left early. | We felt boring during the film. | The film was boring, so we left early. | The bored film sent us to sleep.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The film was boring, so we left early.
quizzes.explanation: A film causes the feeling, so it is boring; the people watching it are the ones who feel bored.

quizzes.question: Which technique from Unit 3 gives human actions to something that is not human?
quizzes.explanation: Personification gives human actions to non-human things, such as saying the wind danced.

quizzes.question: Which Unit 4 word describes someone who is very happy because good news has just arrived?
quizzes.explanation: Elated means very happy about good news; famished means hungry, oblivious means unaware and wary means careful.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is written in the present passive?
quizzes.options: The rangers planted new trees last month. | New trees are planted along the trail every year. | The club will plant trees tomorrow. | Planting trees is enjoyable for everyone.
quizzes.correctAnswer: New trees are planted along the trail every year.
quizzes.explanation: The present passive pairs are with a past participle: trees are planted.

quizzes.question: Which Unit 6 review word names facts or information that help prove a claim is true?
quizzes.explanation: Evidence names the facts that prove a claim; analogy, perseverance and rhythm mean quite different things.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the Unit 7 verb pattern correctly?
quizzes.options: She decided applying for the scholarship. | She enjoys to practise interviews. | She decided to apply for the scholarship. | She finished to write her report.
quizzes.correctAnswer: She decided to apply for the scholarship.
quizzes.explanation: Decide takes to plus the infinitive, so she decided to apply is the only correct pattern.

quizzes.question: Nora said, 'I have just posted the article.' Which reported version is correct?
quizzes.options: Nora said that I had just posted the article. | Nora said me that she had just posted the article. | Nora says that she has just posting the article. | Nora said that she had just posted the article.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Nora said that she had just posted the article.
quizzes.explanation: Reported speech backshifts have posted to had posted and changes the pronoun I to she.

quizzes.question: Which sentence means the same as 'If you do not water the seedlings, they will die.'?
quizzes.options: Unless the seedlings die, you will water them. | Unless you water the seedlings, they will not die. | Unless you water the seedlings, they will die. | If you water the seedlings, they will die.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Unless you water the seedlings, they will die.
quizzes.explanation: Unless means if not, so unless you water them keeps the original warning unchanged.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Check the four pieces span at least three different units and that every annotation quotes one concrete detail as evidence of growth.
Any grouping logic is acceptable if it is named clearly; the connecting sentence must use both chosen words with their taught meanings.
Verify one accurate fact and one genuine opinion per passage; strong answers cite attribution or evidence when naming the most trustworthy text.
Count four given and four received suggestions, each pointing at a specific line; check at least one suggestion was acted on in revision.
The rehearsal log should show two timings near five minutes and three concrete delivery improvements, not general resolutions.
Confirm the product was presented, at least three questions were answered with evidence, and the Grade 8 goal is specific enough to check next year.
infuriate. Unit 1 taught infuriate as to make someone very angry; the other three review words carry no sense of anger.
The film was boring, so we left early. The -ing participle describes the cause of the feeling, as Unit 2 practised.
personification. Giving human actions to something non-human is personification, which Unit 3's poems used constantly.
elated. Unit 4 defined elated as very happy about good news; famished, oblivious and wary describe hunger, inattention and caution.
New trees are planted along the trail every year. The present passive uses are plus the past participle, the Unit 5 focus.
evidence. Unit 6 defined evidence as facts that help prove something true; the other options name different ideas entirely.
She decided to apply for the scholarship. Decide takes to plus the infinitive, one of Unit 7's verb patterns.
Nora said that she had just posted the article. Reported speech backshifts the present perfect and swaps the pronoun, as Unit 8 taught.
Unless you water the seedlings, they will die. Unless means if not, the Unit 9 conditional pattern.
Her honest plans convinced students she would truly act. The retelling of Unit 2's story credits Imani's honest, practical campaign.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "My English Voice: Grade 7 Capstone" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'belligerent'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Review text 1: Keeping the Story Alive (Unit 1)" was about in their own words, and what happened in "Review text 2: The Hero of Kitale (Unit 2)" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Reported speech across the year (Units 8 and 9)" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
